claims.text: An intermediate degree of surface oxidation on PGM nanoparticles creates a dual-function ensemble containing metallic and oxidized sites.
Metallic sites adsorb and dehydrogenate ethanol.
Adjacent moderately oxidized sites promote oxygen activation.
The combined metallic and oxidized sites promote efficient 12-electron/12-proton ethanol oxidation.
Moderately increasing surface oxide coverage without fully passivating the metal enhances ethanol-oxidation performance.
Both insufficient and excessive surface oxidation reduce catalytic effectiveness.
The as-synthesized PGM catalyst has a native thin oxide overlayer.
The as-synthesized catalyst exhibits high ethanol-oxidation performance.
Mild oxidation or reduction treatments can systematically vary the oxide-layer thickness while particle size, dispersion, and support are held constant.
The thickness and continuity of the oxide overlayer or metal–oxide interface mediate dual-site ethanol oxidation.
A balanced metal–oxide interface optimizes activation energies for electron/proton transfer and complete oxidation to CO2.
Optimizing the metal–oxide interface improves selectivity, turnover frequency, and operational durability.
An optimized modest increase in oxide thickness produces higher current density and lower overpotential.
An optimized oxide thickness increases CO2 selectivity and decreases formation of partial-oxidation products such as acetaldehyde.
An optimized oxide thickness improves activity retention during extended operation.
An excessively thick oxide layer decreases activity by hindering electron transfer.
An oxide layer that is too thin provides insufficient oxygen activation.
The proposed relationship applies at moderate temperatures and potentials typical of fuel-cell ethanol oxidation.
The proposed relationship may fail at strongly oxidative or reductive potentials that fully oxidize or reduce the catalyst surface.
The proposed relationship may fail when mass transport is the dominant performance limitation.
